title: Forty-Two
passages:
The handset was where Wren had folded it, a gray rubber brick with a bar on the side that you squeezed to talk and let go to listen. Dey got his thumb over the bar. It took him two tries. The first squeeze gave the deck a half second of open channel and the hiss of the storm, and he let go without a word, the way a man does when he has been about to say something for fourteen hours and finds it has moved somewhere he can't reach.

Wren kept working the bag. Four squeezes to the breath, a pause, four more; the bag was a rubber football with a one-way valve, and she had been at it long enough that her forearm had gone to shaking wire.

"Say it," she said. "Nobody down here is keeping score anymore. Sol's rule. It's in the log and everything."

Dey's lips were the color of the inside of a shell. He keyed the bar.

"Kettle low gate, this is the Marrow." Three words, a stop, three more. "Dey Okafor. I can't breathe. I need the lung rig. I'm asking."

The answer came back before he had let go of the bar. Quill had been sitting on the channel with the berth book open on her knee and the stylus behind her ear, waiting, because waiting was the job.

"Logged at the bell plus ten," she said. "Your name went in the book when you signed and it stays in whether you walk off this deck or not. The book doesn't strike. That's the price and it's already paid."

"Say the rest," Dey said.

"The lavage is a pump and a hose and forty liters of warm water. It flushes what's in your chest out of your chest. It doesn't mend what's torn. I've run it eleven times. Four sat up. Seven didn't, and I logged those too. The rig is lashed on the mole barge at the east mole and she has to cast off, cross the eye, and winch it over your rail. Nine minutes if the ebb lets her and it won't. The channel's shut to you, Marrow. It isn't shut to me."

"Nine minutes," Sol said. She was standing at the rail with her hand on nothing in particular, which was where her hand went when she'd lost the thread of a sentence and didn't want anybody to see her find it again. "Nia. What have we got."

"Six on the deck clock," Nia said, without looking up from the paper log open on her knee. "Dey's got six."

"That's the worst bedside manner on this coast," Dey told the handset.

"It's the only kind I've got," Quill said, and the channel hissed.

Dey dragged the bar down one more time. "Tell your barge I said please. First time in my life. I want it written down somewhere."

"It's written down."

Bayo had come up out of the well with grease to the elbow. He stood with his head cocked east, the way he stood when he was reading water instead of looking at it. "That's her casting off the mole," he said. "Two cylinders, and she knocks on the upstroke. Listen—"

The engine east of them changed note. It came off the knock and went smooth, and the whole sound of it swung, the way a hull swings when the man at the wheel puts the tiller over and the bow starts to come around.

Bayo's face did something small and unhelpful.

"Mole barge turns to starboard to clear the mole head," he said. "That one's coming about to port." He squinted into the rain, where there was nothing to squint at, no lamp, no masthead, no deck light, just the black line of the chop and the tower standing in it. "And she's running dark. Nobody runs dark in the eye unless they don't want to be counted."
